newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia seen avoiding new U.S. blacklisting.
newsitem.headline: Colombia seen avoiding new U.S. blacklisting.

text.p: Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia predicted Friday that Colombia would avoid a new blacklisting by the United States for failing to act aggressively enough in its war against drug trafficking.
"Colombia has demonstrated that it's making serious progress," said Mejia, who returned late Thursday from an official visit to Washington.

Colombia was severely shaken last March when U.S. President Bill Clinton's included it on a list of virtual pariah states -- Afghanistan, Burma, Iran, Nigeria and Syria -- that had failed to cooperate in the international fight against drugs.
In an annual statement required by Congress, Clinton will announce again on Feb. 27 whether Colombia should be "certified" as a trustworth ally in the drug fight.

So-called "decertification" for a second consecutive year could trigger punitive economic sanctions that Clinton fell short of imposing in 1996. In addition to increased tariffs on Colombian exports, Clinton could invoke the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose a wide variety of sanctions, including the suspension of banking services between the United States and Colombia.

In her talks with U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard and other senior officials in Washington, Mejia said it was made abundantly clear that Colombia will not pass the annual drug test with flying colors.
But she predicted that it would revert to the status it had in 1995, when Clinton "certified" Colombia because it was in U.S. "vital national interests" to do so.
"It would be the first time in history that the United States takes a bit of a step back," she said, noting that no country placed on the virtual U.S. blacklist had ever managed to win removal.

U.S. officials say certification decisions are made on drug grounds alone, not for political reasons. But President Ernesto Samper's alleged ties to drug lords, and charges that traffickers had infiltrated his government, were cited among reasons for decertification last year.

Mejia, who spoke in an interview with the RCN radio network, did not mention the dim view Washington still has of Samper. But she said Gelbard and other officials had expressed particular concern about "very strong growth" in drug production in Colombia -- which is the world's leading supplier of cocaine and a top supplier of heroin to the United States.
Colombian police and military officials say they are doing everything possible to fight production. But the scale of it is "strong" indeed.

Just two weeks ago, police announced the dismantling of a huge clandestine drug laboratory, said capable of producing 50 tons of cocaine a month. And Col. Jose Leonardo Gallego, the respected chief of Colombia's anti-narcotics police, said another sprawling drug lab was destroyed early Friday in southeastern Vichada province.
More than 10 tons of pure cocaine were seized in those two busts alone, authorities said.

A Colombian judge's decision to hand down extremely light prison sentences last month to two of the world's biggest drug lords is sure to weigh on the U.S. decision whether to certify Colombia. But the head of Colombia's Senate told Reuters late Friday that proposed legislation increasing sentences for trafficking was likely to be approved by both houses of Congress as early as next week.

And Justice Minister Carlos Medellin said the government would bow to a key U.S. demand in March by proposing that Congress lift Colombia's 5-year-old constitutional ban on extradition. A lifting of the ban could mean that jailed Cali cartel kingpins will eventually be put on trial in the United States, he said.

In a Reuter interview Thursday night, Samper said anything but certification of his government's anti-drug efforts would be "highly demoralizing." He also stressed that another year of decertification would be sure to add to growing anti-American sentiment in Colombia, a country where he said leftist "narcoguerrillas" made up to $700 million from the drug trade last year.

U.S. officials have played down what Samper and senior Colombian military officials have long maintained to be a direct link between the drug trade and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Colombia's largest and oldest guerrilla group.
